0.title: Obadiah: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
0.overview:
Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament: one chapter, twenty-one verses. We know nothing about the prophet apart from his name. Yet this small book asks a question every believer eventually asks. What does God do about the people who stood by, or even cheered, while his people suffered?

The message concerns Edom, and Edom and Israel were family. The Edomites descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob. The conflict began before the brothers were born, when God said to their mother, Two nations are in your womb (Gen 25:23). Esau sold his birthright, lost his father's blessing and hated Jacob (Gen 27:41). The two men were later reconciled (Gen 33:4), but their descendants nursed the quarrel for a thousand years, even though God's law told Israel, You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother (Deut 23:7).

When Jerusalem fell, Edom watched, cheered, looted and caught the refugees. Psalm 137 remembers it with tears: Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem (Ps 137:7). Obadiah is God's answer.

Most place Obadiah soon after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, since verses 11-14 read like an eyewitness account; others place him in the ninth century BC. Much of the book runs parallel to Jeremiah 49:7-22. Nothing in the message depends on these questions.

The book falls into three parts. Verses 1-9 announce Edom's fall and expose its cause: The pride of your heart has deceived you (v. 3). Verses 10-14 bring the charge: the violence done to your brother Jacob. Edom stood aloof, and God's verdict on the bystander is devastating: you were like one of them (v. 11). Verses 15-21 lift the horizon to the day of the LORD upon all the nations, and end with rescue on Mount Zion and the promise that the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

Three themes run through the book. Pride deceives. Edom trusted its cliff fortresses, wealth, allies and advisers, and God stripped away every one. God watches how we treat one another. The sins named here are not exotic: looking on, feeling pleased, saying something, then joining in. God repays. The rule of his day is As you have done, it shall be done to you (v. 15). Jesus said the same: with the measure you use it will be measured to you (Matt 7:2).

That last theme would leave us all without hope, because none of us could survive a judgment that handed back exactly what we have given others. This is why Obadiah's picture of a cup matters (v. 16). In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39). At the cross he received what we had done, so that we might receive what he deserved. He also fulfils the book's last promise. Obadiah says Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion (v. 21); the New Testament tells believers, you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Heb 12:22, 24). At the end the announcement rings out, The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ (Rev 11:15).

Obadiah's severity toward a nation is not God's last word to its people. Amos heard God promise that the restored kingdom of David would include the remnant of Edom (Amos 9:12), and the apostles saw that promise coming true as Gentiles turned to Christ (Acts 15:16-17). Centuries after Obadiah, Herod the Great, a king of Edomite descent, tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matt 2:16). Edom is long gone; the King it tried to kill reigns still.

So this little book speaks to anyone who has been wronged and wondered whether God noticed, and to anyone tempted to enjoy an enemy's downfall. Those who have been shown mercy at the cross need not be proud, for God brings the high down, nor gloat, for he is watching how we treat our brothers. And they need not fear the powers that look unshakeable, because the last word of Obadiah is also the last word of history: the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Pride of Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God summons the nations against Edom (vv. 1-2). Proud in its rock fortresses, Edom will be brought down (vv. 3-4), stripped bare and betrayed by its allies (vv. 5-7), its wisdom and its soldiers failing (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride deceives, and no height, wealth or cleverness can keep anyone safe from God.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord GOD concerning Edom: We have heard a report from the LORD, and a messenger has been sent among the nations: "Rise up! Let us rise against her for battle!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know nothing about Obadiah except his name: no king, no date, no family. What we have is a vision from God concerning Edom.

Most date the book soon after 586 BC, when the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem, because verses 11-14 describe foreigners casting lots for the city while Edom looked on. Psalm 137 remembers that day and prays, Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem (Ps 137:7). Others believe he preached much earlier, in the ninth century BC (about 845 BC), when Edom rebelled against Judah (2 Kgs 8:20-22) and raiders plundered Jerusalem and the royal household (2 Chr 21:16-17). Nothing in the message depends on settling it.

Much of Obadiah is very like Jeremiah 49:7-22. Some think Jeremiah drew on Obadiah, some the reverse, and others that both used an older oracle about Edom; the message is the same either way.

The prophet has overheard heaven's news: a messenger is stirring up the nations for war against Edom. Nations imagine they choose their own wars. Obadiah shows us who is actually moving the pieces.
verseByVerse.note: The name Obadiah means "servant of the LORD"; about a dozen different men in the Old Testament bear it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make you small among the nations; you shall be utterly despised. The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock, in your lofty dwelling, who say in your heart, "Who will bring me down to the ground?" Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom's future is settled in one sentence. (The ESV notes that it may be read as already accomplished: "Behold, I have made you small".)

Who were the Edomites? They were the descendants of Esau, Jacob's twin brother (Gen 36:1). The feud began before the twins were born, when God said, Two nations are in your womb (Gen 25:23). Esau sold his birthright, lost the blessing, and hated Jacob (Gen 27:41). The brothers were later reconciled, and Esau ran to meet Jacob, embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him (Gen 33:4). But their descendants kept the quarrel alive for a thousand years. Edom refused Israel passage on the way to the promised land (Num 20:18), even though God's law said, You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother (Deut 23:7).

Readers who know Malachi's words, I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated (Mal 1:2-3), which Paul uses of God's free choice in grace (Rom 9:13), may wonder whether Edom was simply doomed from birth. Obadiah does not argue that way. He names what Edom did, its pride and its cruelty to a brother, and judges it for that. God's free choice and real human guilt stand side by side in Scripture, and neither cancels the other.

Here is the heart of the matter: pride is a liar. It tells us we are safe, self-sufficient and beyond correction, and by the time we discover otherwise it is too late.

Edom's pride had a geographical basis. The people lived in the clefts of the rock (the ESV notes this may be a place name, "Sela", meaning a rock stronghold), in the high red sandstone country southeast of the Dead Sea, on cliffs reached through narrow gorges; the rock city of Petra, carved by a later people, lies in that region. It is one thing to feel secure; it is another to say in your heart that nobody, not even God, can touch you.

However high the eagle builds, God reaches higher. The same charge was laid against Babylon, whose king said, I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high (Isa 14:13). Height is no defence when God is the one who brings you down.

Every reader needs this. Our fortresses are usually not cliffs but savings, qualifications, reputation, health or family. None of them are wrong in themselves, and all of them can quietly become the answer to the question "Who will bring me down?" God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). Jesus said, everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 18:14). It is far better to come down willingly now, into the arms of the God who gives grace to the humble, than to be brought down at the last.
verseByVerse.note: Sela is probably the rock stronghold that King Amaziah of Judah captured and renamed Joktheel (2 Kgs 14:7).

verseByVerse.quote: If thieves came to you, if plunderers came by night— how you have been destroyed!— would they not steal only enough for themselves? If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? How Esau has been pillaged, his treasures sought out! All your allies have driven you to your border; those at peace with you have deceived you; they have prevailed against you; those who eat your bread have set a trap beneath you— you have no understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obadiah uses two pictures from ordinary life. Thieves take what they can carry and leave the rest; grape pickers always miss a few bunches, and the poor came behind to gather them. Even a robbery and a harvest leave something behind. But when God deals with Edom, nothing will be left. Their hidden treasures, stored in caves and cliff strongholds, will be sought out. The prophet breaks into the middle of his own sentence with a cry: how you have been destroyed! He speaks as if it has already happened, because God has said it.

Edom sat on important trade routes and knew how to make friends with the strong. Now those friends, the ones at the dinner table, set the trap. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew of this line is compressed, so that the words those who eat are supplied, and that it reads "he has set a trap".) Edom, who betrayed a brother, is betrayed by friends. In time Edom was indeed driven out of its ancient territory, probably by Arab peoples such as the Nabataeans in the centuries after the exile, and had to settle further west in southern Judah, which came to be called Idumea.

Edom was famous for its clever men, and it had no understanding of this. Worldly shrewdness can arrange everything except an answer to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Will I not on that day, declares the LORD, destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of Mount Esau? And your mighty men shall be dismayed, O Teman, so that every man from Mount Esau will be cut off by slaughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom had a reputation for wisdom. Jeremiah asks, Is wisdom no more in Teman? (Jer 49:7), and Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite, from Edomite territory (Job 2:11). Wisdom is God's gift, and he can withdraw it. A nation can lose the ability to think clearly about its own danger.

The mighty men will be dismayed, their courage gone before the battle. One layer at a time God takes away the cliffs (vv. 3-4), the hidden treasure (vv. 5-6), the allies (v. 7), the wise men (v. 8), and now the soldiers. It is a sober picture of what happens when God finally deals with human pride: not a fair fight, but a quiet collapse.
verseByVerse.note: Teman, named after a grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11), often stands for Edom as a whole.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Day of Your Brother
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The charge is violence against your brother Jacob: on the day Jerusalem fell, Edom stood aloof and was like one of them (vv. 10-11). Eight commands name what Edom did, from gloating to cutting off the fugitives (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Standing by while others suffer, and gloating over a brother's ruin, are sins God takes personally.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever. On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were like one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The key word in the charge is brother. God had protected Edom's land when Israel marched to Canaan and forbidden Israel to despise them. Edom's violence was against family.

God notices what families and churches do to their own. The closer the tie, the deeper the wound, and the more seriously he takes it.

Here is the scene: Jerusalem has fallen. Foreign soldiers pour through the broken gates, carry off everything of value and gamble for the city as if it were a prize. And where was Edom? You stood aloof. They did not swing a sword in that sentence. They simply stood and watched their brother being destroyed.

In God's eyes the bystander had joined the attackers. Standing aside is a choice. It was the sin of the priest and the Levite who crossed the road and left the wounded man (Luke 10:31-32), and it is the sin John describes when he asks how God's love can be in a person who sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him (1 John 3:17). Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (Jas 4:17).

verseByVerse.quote: But do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune; do not rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their ruin; do not boast in the day of distress. Do not enter the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; do not gloat over his disaster in the day of his calamity; do not loot his wealth in the day of his calamity. Do not stand at the crossroads to cut off his fugitives; do not hand over his survivors in the day of distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word day beats through these eight commands like a drum. God is not giving Edom advice for next time; each command is a photograph of a crime.

Watch the progression, because it is the way sin always grows. It begins in the eyes: do not gloat. Then it reaches the heart: do not rejoice. Then it comes out of the mouth: do not boast (the ESV notes the Hebrew is vivid, "do not enlarge your mouth"). Then the feet move: Do not enter the gate of my people. Then the hands take: do not loot his wealth. Finally the worst of all: standing at the crossroads to catch the refugees running for their lives, and handing the survivors over to the enemy. What began as a look ended in murder.

In the middle of this God calls Judah my people. Even in the hour when he was judging them, they were still his, and he was watching how others treated them.

This is the searching part of Obadiah for ordinary readers. Few of us will ever plunder a city. But the quiet pleasure at the downfall of someone we resent, the colleague who failed, the church that split, the family member whose marriage collapsed, is the very sin God names first. Scripture says plainly, Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles (Prov 24:17). The gloating heart is only the beginning, but it is a real beginning. When we find that pleasure in ourselves, the answer is not to despair but to confess it to the Christ who prayed for those who mocked him (Luke 23:34), and whose Spirit teaches us to weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day of the LORD comes on all nations, and each will be repaid (vv. 15-16). But Zion will have survivors and be holy (vv. 17-18), God's people will possess the land (vv. 19-20), and the kingdom shall be the LORD's (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends not with Edom or any empire, but with salvation on Mount Zion and the kingdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you; your deeds shall return on your own head. For as you have drunk on my holy mountain, so all the nations shall drink continually; they shall drink and swallow, and shall be as though they had never been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message suddenly widens from one small nation to all the nations. Edom is a sample case. What God does to Edom, he will do to every proud and cruel power, because he is the God of the whole earth.

The rule of that day is simple. Edom cut off fugitives, and Edom will be cut off (v. 9). Edom looted, and Edom will be pillaged (v. 6). Jesus stated the same principle: with the measure you use it will be measured to you (Matt 7:2), and Paul warned, whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7).

None of us would survive a judgment that gave us back exactly what we have given others. This is why the gospel is such good news.

The word drunk may look back to Edom celebrating on my holy mountain, God's temple hill, while Jerusalem burned; it is a picture of revelling in another's ruin. It may also point forward to the cup of God's wrath that the prophets often describe: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine (Ps 75:8), which God made the nations drink (Jer 25:15-17). Most likely both are in view: they drank in triumph, and now they will drink judgment. The end is total: they will be as though they had never been.

The only way to escape that cup is that Someone else drank it. At the cross, Christ received what we had done, so that we might receive what he deserved. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39), and then said, shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? (John 18:11). He drank it to the dregs for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: But in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess their own possessions. The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall burn them and consume them, and there shall be no survivor for the house of Esau, for the LORD has spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment is not the last word. But is one of the great words of the Bible. On the hill where Edom had celebrated, God will keep a rescued people. Joel had said the same: in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape (Joel 2:32), and he added the promise that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved.

Zion shall be holy, cleansed of everything that defiled it, and God's people will get back what was taken from them. Believers have already come to that Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Heb 12:22, 24).

Edom had seemed as permanent as its cliffs; before God's people it will prove as flimsy as dry stubble before a flame. The house of Jacob and the house of Joseph are the southern and northern tribes together, reunited in God's purpose.

These are hard words, and honesty requires us to feel their weight. They are God's sentence on a nation that had shown no mercy, and Edom did eventually disappear as a people. Yet even here the door is not shut against individual Edomites: the restored kingdom of David would include the remnant of Edom (Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16-17). The nation that fought God's people perished; sinners from every nation, including Israel's old enemies, are welcomed in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Those of the Negeb shall possess Mount Esau, and those of the Shephelah shall possess the land of the Philistines; they shall possess the land of Ephraim and the land of Samaria, and Benjamin shall possess Gilead. The exiles of this host of the people of Israel shall possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and the exiles of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad shall possess the cities of the Negeb. Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verses sweep around the compass. The Negeb is the dry south, the Shephelah the low hills west toward Philistia, Ephraim and Samaria the central highlands, and Gilead the land east of the Jordan. Zarephath lay up the coast in Phoenicia, where Elijah once stayed with a widow (1 Kgs 17:9). Sepharad is a place we cannot identify with certainty; it has often been connected with Sardis in Asia Minor, and Jewish readers in the Middle Ages took it to mean Spain, which is why Jews of Spanish descent are still called Sephardic. The point of the list is not geography but reversal: the people who lost everything will be given more than they lost, and the scattered exiles will come home.

Saviors is the word used for the deliverers God raised up in the days of the judges (Judg 3:9; Neh 9:27): men who rescued his people when they cried to him. From Zion they rule the proud height that thought itself untouchable.

The book ends in one magnificent line, which is the point of the whole book. The kingdom belongs not to Edom, Babylon or any power that seems to own the future, but to God, and one day everyone will see it. Zechariah says it too: the LORD will be king over all the earth (Zech 14:9).

The New Testament shows us how it comes about. There is one Savior who went up to Mount Zion, and he is the Lord himself. Jesus Christ was crucified outside Jerusalem, rose, and ascended to reign, and at the end the announcement rings out, The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever (Rev 11:15). Centuries after Obadiah, Herod the Great, a king of Edomite descent, tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matt 2:16). Esau's line made one last attempt on the child of Jacob's line, and failed. Within about a century the Idumeans, as Edom's descendants were then called, had vanished from history; the King they tried to kill reigns forever.

So this little book leaves the believer, who has been shown mercy, with three things. Do not be proud, because God brings the high down. Do not gloat over anyone's fall, because God is watching how we treat our brothers. And do not fear the Edoms of this world, however secure they look: the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

How is the possession of these lands fulfilled? Partly in the return after the exile; fully in Christ’s kingdom, where his people inherit the earth (Matt 5:5). Dispensationalists look for a literal future possession by Israel, because they read the land promises as still awaiting fulfilment for the nation; this commentary reads them, with the New Testament, as widened in Christ to the whole earth (Rom 4:13), and gladly acknowledges that faithful Christians differ here. The “saviors” of verse 21 are deliverers God raises up, fulfilled in Christ and in his people who share his reign (Rev 3:21); the kingdom shall be the LORD’s has begun in Christ and will be complete when he returns.

1.title: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
1.overview:
Obadiah's one chapter moves in three steps. First God announces that proud Edom, safe in its cliffs, will be brought down (vv. 1-9). Then he names the reason: when Jerusalem fell, Edom stood by, gloated and joined in against its own brother (vv. 10-14).

Finally the view widens to the day of the LORD on all nations, and the book ends not with Edom's ruin but with rescue on Mount Zion and the promise that the kingdom shall be the LORD's (vv. 15-21).
1.theology:
God rules the nations and moves them as he wills, even when they think they are choosing their own wars (v. 1).

Pride deceives; no fortress, wealth or cleverness can protect anyone from God, who opposes the proud (vv. 3-4, 8-9; Isa 14:13-14; Jas 4:6; Luke 18:14).

God takes wrongs done within the family of his people personally, and counts the bystander among the attackers (vv. 10-11; Luke 10:31-32; 1 John 3:17; Jas 4:17).

Gloating over another's downfall is sin, and it is where cruelty begins (vv. 12-14; Prov 24:17-18).

God repays what people have done, and Christ drank the cup of that judgment in his people's place (vv. 15-16; Matt 7:2; Gal 6:7; Ps 75:8; Matt 26:39; John 18:11).

God preserves a people who escape, and makes Zion holy; believers have come to the heavenly Zion in Christ (v. 17; Joel 2:32; Heb 12:22-24).

Judgment on hostile nations and mercy to individuals from them belong together: a remnant of Edom is promised to the kingdom of David's Son (v. 18; Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16-17).

History ends with salvation on Mount Zion and with God's kingdom, established by Jesus Christ, the true Savior and King (v. 21; Judg 3:9; Zech 14:9; Rev 11:15).
1.examples:
Edom nested in its cliffs and asked who could ever bring it down. God answered by taking away, one by one, everything it trusted, until even the friends at its table set a trap for it. Our own fortresses are more often savings, reputation or health than rock, and they can be held humbly or proudly.

Edom's sin began with a brother standing at a distance, watching a city burn; the look became a cheer, the cheer a robbery, and the robbery ended with refugees caught at the crossroads. The quiet pleasure we take in someone's fall is the same sin at its beginning, and it can be confessed to the Christ who prayed for those who mocked him.

The cup Edom passed round in triumph became the cup of judgment, and Christ drank that cup for his people. So the book ends not with stubble where a fortress stood but with saviors on Zion and a kingdom that belongs to God alone.
